How does the JB Hi-Fi database enforce its business rules?

Long image

A

Answer

All 22 business rules live inside PostgreSQL, not in the API. Rules that one row can decide are constraints; rules that must read other rows are triggers. Every failure carries its brNN_… name, and the API returns that name as a 409 error code.

  1. Keys, domains, CHECK and UNIQUE decide single-row rules; composite foreign keys add “same order”, “same customer” and “same store”.1
  2. Triggers handle rules that read other rows: they run before the write and raise SQLSTATE 23514 with the rule's name.2
  3. Where two transactions could both pass a check, the trigger first locks a row both need, so the checks run one after the other.2
  4. app/errors.py turns that name into the API's error code, and a test breaks every rule on purpose.3

Applies toCommit 4d49cf5sql/ and app/PostgreSQL 18

1

How was the database designed?

Diagram structure
  • Requirements R1–R14 req
  • Business rules BR01–BR22 br
  • ER model er
  • Tables and keys tables
  • Constraints and triggers enforce
  • A test per rule tests
  • br → er
  • enforce → tests · 409 code
  • er → tables · map
  • req → br
  • tables → enforce · brNN_ names
  1. Requirements R1–R14 ↗

    What customers and staff must do: browse, order, return, adjust stock, read reports.

  2. Business rules BR01–BR22 ↗

    Each rule keeps a permanent ID, so it can be traced to its constraint, its test and the report.

  3. ER model ↗

    Strong and weak entities, one ISA, one recursive and one M:N relationship with an attribute.

  4. Tables and keys ↗

    Derived values become views, not columns. One BCNF break is deliberate: return_line.order_id.

  5. Constraints and triggers ↗

    One-row rules become constraints; rules over other rows become triggers. Each object is named brNN_….

  6. A test per rule ↗

    tests/test_business_rules.py breaks each rule and asserts its name; tests/test_rule_traceability.py checks the rule table against the catalog.

What does the schema look like?

Diagram structure
  • user_account user_account
  • staff staff
  • store store
  • customer customer
  • customer_address customer_address
  • order_status_transition order_status_transition
  • order_status_history order_status_history
  • customer_order customer_order
  • order_line order_line
  • return_request return_request
  • return_line return_line
  • payment payment
  • inventory inventory

  • brand brand

  • product_spec product_spec
  • promotion promotion
  • user_account → customer
  • user_account → staff
  • staff → store · works at
  • store → staff · managed by
  • customer_address → customer
  • customer_order → customer
  • customer_order → customer_address · delivers to
  • customer_order → store · fulfilled at
  • order_line → customer_order
  • order_line → product
  • order_status_history → customer_order
  • order_status_history → staff · changed by
  • return_request → customer_order
  • return_request → store · received at
  • return_request → staff · processed by
  • return_request → staff · resolved by

  • stock_adjustment → staff · made by
  • product → brand
  • product → category
  • product_spec → product

  1. customer_address ↗

    Weak entity: its key (customer_id, address_no) includes the owner's key. order_line, order_status_history and product_spec follow the same pattern.

  2. inventory ↗

    The M:N relationship between store and product, with quantity as its attribute. Its key is (store_id, product_id).

  3. staff ↗

    The ISA (store employee or support staff) is one table with staff_type. BR05's CHECK requires a store exactly for store staff.

  4. store ↗

    manager_id must work at this store. The composite FK to staff is checked at COMMIT, because store and staff point at each other.

  5. user_account ↗

    A sign-in belongs to one customer or one staff member: two unique FKs and an XOR CHECK (BR19).

  6. customer_order ↗

    After insert only status may change (BR09). The total is not stored: v_order_total computes it from the lines.

  7. order_line ↗

    unit_price records the price at sale time, a different fact from today's base_price. Lines are never edited (BR08).

  8. return_line ↗

    It repeats order_id on purpose. The composite FK to return_request (return_id, order_id) then proves the line comes from the returned order (BR13).

3

Which mechanism enforces each rule?

RuleWhat it saysEnforced by
BR01Customer email is unique and well-formedUNIQUE (email); email_address domain CHECK
BR02Money is never negative and has two decimalsmoney_aud domain: NUMERIC(10,2) with CHECK (VALUE >= 0)
BR03Stock never goes negativeCHECK (quantity >= 0) on inventory
BR04Each store has one manager, who works theremanager_id NOT NULL and a composite FK to staff, deferred to COMMIT
BR05Store staff have one store; support staff have noneCHECK ((staff_type = 'support') = (store_id IS NULL))
BR06Delivery needs an address; Click & Collect has none and uses a retail storeCHECK, plus a trigger on the order side and one on the store side
BR07Quantity above 0, each product once, still on sale, at least one lineCHECK, UNIQUE, a BEFORE INSERT trigger, a deferred constraint trigger
BR08An order line is a purchase recordBEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE trigger and a TRUNCATE guard
BR09Status follows the allowed moves, and every change is loggedTransition table read by a BEFORE trigger; an AFTER trigger writes history; guards keep it append-only
BR10A retried request creates at most one order or returnUNIQUE (customer_id, idempotency_key) and UNIQUE (order_id, idempotency_key)
BR11Returns only for completed orders, within 30 daysBEFORE trigger that reads order_status_history
BR12Returned quantity never exceeds the quantity boughtBEFORE trigger that locks the order line
BR13A return line comes from the returned orderComposite FK (return_id, order_id) to return_request
BR14Each refund is for a return or a cancellation, never above the charge; payments are append-onlyUNIQUE, CHECK, three BEFORE INSERT triggers, append-only triggers
BR15Promotions never overlap; the sale price stays below the base priceA trigger on promotion and one on product
BR16Addresses are never editedBEFORE UPDATE trigger
BR17A delivery address is the customer's own, current addressComposite FK and a BEFORE INSERT trigger
BR18Stock changes are logged by staff of that storeComposite FK, a reason-and-sign CHECK, an append-only trigger
BR19A sign-in is one customer or one staff member, never bothXOR CHECK and two UNIQUE constraints
BR20Paid only when charged exactly the total, once, while placedTwo triggers and a partial unique index
BR21Cancelled only when refunds equal chargesBEFORE UPDATE trigger that reads v_order_payment
BR22Returns are received at a retail store, by its staffTrigger and composite FKs to staff

The full table, with the tests that break each rule, is docs/rule-traceability.md.3

4

What happens when checkout marks an order paid?

Diagram structure
  • Checkout service svc
  • customer_order ord
  • BEFORE triggers trg
  • order_status_history hist
  • Error handler api
  • Storefront web
  • svc → ord · UPDATE status = 'paid'
  • ord → trg · fire in name order
  • trg → ord · all pass: RETURN NEW
  • ord → hist · AFTER trigger logs the move
  • svc → ord · COMMIT runs deferred br07
  • trg → svc · RAISE 23514 with rule name
  • svc → api · IntegrityError, rolled back
  • api → web · 409, code = rule name
  1. BEFORE triggers ↗

    br09_order_header_immutable, br09_order_status_transition, br20_paid_in_full and br21_cancelled_order_refunded run in name order. An illegal move therefore fails as BR09 before BR20 checks money.

  2. order_status_history ↗

    br09_log_status_change inserts the next seq, with the staff member from app.staff_id. A guard refuses rows that no trigger wrote.

  3. customer_order ↗

    At COMMIT, the deferred br07_order_has_lines confirms the order has at least one line.

  4. Error handler ↗

    It reads e.diag.constraint_name and answers 409 with that name as code. Nothing from the transaction is kept.

Triggers on the same event fire in alphabetical order of their names, so the rule names also set the order of the checks.4 The service commits only if every statement succeeds; any error rolls back the whole request.5

5

What does a trigger look like?

Trigger kindWhen it runsUsed for
BEFORE row triggerBefore each row is written; raising an error stops the statementThe checks of BR06–BR22
AFTER row triggerAfter the row is writtenbr09_log_status_change writes the history row
Constraint trigger, DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERREDAt COMMITbr07_order_has_lines: lines are inserted after their order
Statement trigger, BEFORE TRUNCATEOnce per TRUNCATE, which skips row triggersAppend-only tables: payments, history, stock log, order and return lines

Every trigger ends with RAISE EXCEPTION … USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation', CONSTRAINT = 'brNN_…'.2 To the API, a trigger rule then looks exactly like a CHECK violation.7 PostgreSQL has no multi-table assertion, so BR12 and BR20 emulate one with a trigger.8

Which status moves does BR09 allow?

Diagram structure
  • placed placed
  • paid paid
  • picking picking
  • shipped shipped
  • delivered delivered
  • ready ready
  • collected collected
  • cancelled cancelled
  • placed → paid · charged
  • paid → picking · pick
  • picking → shipped · delivery
  • shipped → delivered · arrived
  • picking → ready · Click & Collect
  • ready → collected · picked up
  • placed → cancelled · cancel
  • paid → cancelled · cancel
  • ready → cancelled · not collected

The allowed moves are 13 rows of data, not code: 6 for delivery and 7 for Click & Collect.6 Adding a move is an INSERT, and the cancellation-refund trigger reads the same table. Two moves carry extra gates: BR20 on placed → paid and BR21 on any move to cancelled.9

7

Why do some triggers lock a row first?

RaceWithout protectionWhat stops it
Two checkouts want the last unitBoth read 1 and both sell itUPDATE inventory … WHERE quantity >= n: the second waits, re-checks, updates 0 rows and gets 409 out_of_stock. BR03 is the backstop.
A double click on Place orderTwo ordersUNIQUE (customer_id, idempotency_key) with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: the second request returns the first order (BR10)
Two overlapping promotions at onceEach check sees no overlap (write skew)BR15's trigger locks the product FOR UPDATE; the second waits, then fails
Two returns for the last units of a lineBoth pass the quantity capBR12's trigger locks the order line FOR UPDATE
Two refunds for one orderRefunds exceed the chargeBR14's trigger locks the order FOR UPDATE
A line added while the order turns paidBR20 checks a total without that lineBR08 and BR20 triggers lock the order row
A Click & Collect order while the store becomes a warehouseBoth commitBR06 reads the store FOR SHARE, so the store update waits

The lock works under READ COMMITTED because, after waiting, the trigger's next query takes a fresh snapshot and sees the other commit.10 Rows are locked in one order, the order row first and then inventory by ascending product_id, so two transactions cannot deadlock.11 docs/concurrency-evidence.md runs each faulty pattern beside ours and records what PostgreSQL reports.12

8

How do you answer the usual design questions?

QuestionAnswer
Why triggers and not CHECK constraints?A CHECK sees only the row being written. BR11, BR12, BR14, BR15 and BR20 read other rows, and PostgreSQL has no CREATE ASSERTION.
Why store unit_price when product has base_price?It is the price at sale time, a different fact. There is no dependency product → unit_price, so it is not redundancy.
Why are order totals not stored?A total is derived data. v_order_total computes it from the lines, so it can never disagree with them.
Doesn't return_line.order_id break BCNF?Yes: return_id → order_id. The composite FK to return_request makes a wrong copy impossible, and it enforces BR13 without a trigger.
How is the staff ISA mapped?One table with a staff_type discriminator. BR05's CHECK ties store_id to the type.
Why is the manager FK deferred?store and staff reference each other. A new store and its manager go in one transaction, so the FK is checked at COMMIT.
Why UNIQUE (store_id, staff_id) if staff_id is the key?It gives composite FKs a target, “staff member X of store S”, for BR04, BR18 and BR22.
Why keep status moves in a table?The BR09 trigger only looks the move up. Changing the workflow is a data change, not a code change.
Who writes order_status_history?Only the AFTER trigger. A pg_trigger_depth() guard refuses direct inserts, and other triggers block updates and deletes.
Why not an exclusion constraint for BR15?It needs the btree_gist extension, which is beyond the unit. The trigger locks the product and checks for overlap instead.
Why READ COMMITTED and not SERIALIZABLE?Targeted locks already serialise the risky checks. SERIALIZABLE would abort one transaction with 40001, and every service would need a retry loop.
Why can't an address be edited?Old orders point at it. Editing means retiring it with is_active and adding a new row (BR16); BR17 refuses retired addresses for new orders.

Answers about READ COMMITTED follow the project's own evidence and argument.13
